stages.title: What engineers design and build
stages.hook: Look around you. Who made the bridge, the bike and the bus? Think of one thing that a person had to plan first.
explain: Engineers plan and make things that help people. They build bridges, bikes, buses, pumps and toys.
An engineer first finds a problem. Then she draws a plan. Then she makes it and tests it. If it fails, she fixes it.
Mechanical engineers work with things that move. Wheels, gears and engines are their tools.
Safe is the first rule. A bridge must not fall. A bike must not break.

example.q: People need to cross a river. What can an engineer do?
steps: Find the problem: the river is in the way.
Plan a bridge and draw it.
Build it and test that it is strong.

analogies.home: A chair, a tap and a door hinge were all planned by someone.
analogies.city: Buses, lifts and bridges are made by engineers.
analogies.farm: A tractor and a water pump help farmers. Engineers made them.
analogies.sea: A boat must float and be strong. Engineers plan it.

terms: A person who plans and builds useful things.
A thing that helps us do work.
A plan for how to make something.
Trying something to see if it works.

misc.right: Engineers also plan and make new things, and they test that they are safe.

stages.limits: Engineers work in teams. Many jobs are shared.

trip.prompt: Find a picture of something an engineer made. What does it help people do?

questions.q: What does an engineer do?
o: Paints pictures for a museum all day
questions.why: Engineers plan, make and test things that help people.

questions.q: Which thing did an engineer plan?
questions.why: Bridges are made by people. Clouds, mountains and rivers are made by nature.

questions.q: What should an engineer do after building a bike?
o: Paint it and never ride it
questions.why: Testing shows whether the bike is safe.

questions.q: A bridge must be what?
questions.why: People cross the bridge, so it must not fall.

questions.q: A chair keeps breaking. What should the engineer do?
o: Find why it breaks and fix the design
Sit on it more to test it
Make the legs thinner and lighter to save wood
questions.why: Engineers find the cause of the failure and then improve the plan.

questions.q: Mechanical engineers work with things that do what?
questions.why: Wheels, gears and engines all move.

questions.q: Why do engineers draw a plan first?
o: So the idea is clear before making it
To hide the problem from everyone else
questions.why: A plan helps find mistakes early.

questions.q: Which is the first rule of engineering?
questions.why: A thing that hurts people is a bad design, however fast or shiny.

questions.q: Put the engineer's steps in order.
questions.why: We must know the problem, then plan, then make and test.

questions.q: Match the helper to the job.
questions.why: Each machine solves a different problem.

panel.q: A new toy has a sharp edge. What should the engineers do?
o: Change the design to make it safe
Sell it anyway and hope for the best
Paint the edge a bright colour
panel.why: Safety is fixed in the design, not left to chance.

panel.q: Why do engineers test with small models before building a big bridge?
o: Mistakes are cheaper and safer to find
Models are always prettier than bridges
Big bridges never fail at all
panel.why: Finding a fault in a model costs little and hurts nobody.

panel.q: A water pump in a village stops. What is the best first step?
panel.why: Engineers look for the cause first, then repair.

teach.model: An engineer is a person who makes useful things. She finds a problem, draws a plan, builds it and tests it. For example, she can build a bridge so people cross a river safely.

points.ask: What does she do before she builds?
Then what does she do?
How does she know it is safe?
Can you tell me something an engineer made?

stages.title: Simple machines
stages.hook: How can a small child lift a heavy box up to a truck? Think about a ramp.
explain: A simple machine makes a job easier. It does not do the job by itself.
There are six simple machines: the lever, the pulley, the wheel and axle, the ramp, the wedge and the screw.
A ramp lets you push a box up a slope. The push is smaller, but the path is longer.
Machines change how we push or pull. They can make the push smaller or point it a new way.

example.q: A heavy barrel must go up onto a truck. What simple machine can help?
steps: The barrel is too heavy to lift straight up.
Put a long ramp against the truck.
Roll the barrel up the slope.

analogies.home: A screw holds a shelf. A knife is a wedge.
analogies.city: A ramp helps wheelchairs and prams up a kerb.
analogies.farm: A wheelbarrow and a spade are simple machines.
analogies.sport: A slide and a seesaw are simple machines.

stages.mnemonic: Six helpers: Lever, Pulley, Wheel, Ramp, Wedge, Screw.
terms: A tool that makes work easier.
A sloping surface. Also called an inclined plane.
Two ramps joined to cut or split.
A ramp wrapped around a rod.

misc.wrong: A machine does the work for free.
misc.right: A machine only makes the job easier to push or pull. We still do the work.

stages.limits: Real machines have rubbing, called friction, so they are never perfect.

trip.prompt: Find the six simple machines. Which one have you used today?

questions.q: What does a simple machine do?
questions.why: Simple machines help us push or pull more easily.

questions.q: Which is a ramp?
o: A sloping board to roll a box up
A round wheel that spins on a rod
A rope hung on a hook
questions.why: A ramp is a slope, also called an inclined plane.

questions.q: A knife cuts bread. What simple machine is the blade?
questions.why: A blade is a thin wedge that pushes things apart.

questions.q: A screw is like a ramp that is what?
questions.why: The thread of a screw is a ramp that winds around.

questions.q: You must lift a barrel onto a truck. Which choice is easier on your muscles?
questions.why: A longer slope needs a smaller push, though the path is longer.

questions.q: How many simple machines are in the usual list?
questions.why: Lever, pulley, wheel and axle, ramp, wedge and screw make six.

questions.q: Which is NOT a simple machine?
questions.why: A cloud is not a tool people make.

questions.q: Why is a ramp good for a wheelchair?
o: The slope needs less push than a big step
The slope is shorter than a step
It makes the chair weigh less
It makes the chair float up the slope easily
questions.why: A gentle slope spreads the lift over a longer path.

questions.q: Put the ramps from easiest push to hardest push.
questions.why: The gentler the slope, the smaller the push needed.

questions.q: Match the machine to its use.
questions.why: Each simple machine has a clear job.

panel.q: Does a ramp make the path shorter or longer?
o: It has no path at all
panel.why: A slope is longer than the straight height, which is why the push is smaller.

panel.q: A girl says, "A machine gives me free work." What is the best reply?
o: It makes work easier but is not free
She is exactly right, work is free
Machines never help anybody at all
panel.why: Machines change the push or direction, not the need for effort.

panel.q: An axe splits a log. Why is a thin edge better than a flat one?
o: A thin wedge pushes into wood easily
A flat edge is sharper than a thin one
panel.why: A narrow edge puts the push on a tiny spot.

teach.model: A simple machine is a tool that makes a job easier. A ramp is one. It lets you push a heavy box up a slope instead of lifting it. It does not do the work for you, but it helps.

points.ask: What does a simple machine do?
Can you name one?
What does it change for us?
Can you give me an example?

stages.title: Levers and pulleys
stages.hook: Why is it easy to open a paint tin with a spoon handle? Where do you put your push?
explain: A lever is a stiff bar that turns on a point. The point is called the pivot or fulcrum.
A seesaw is a lever. Push down on one end and the other end goes up.
A long lever helps lift heavy things. The longer the bar on your side, the less you push.
A pulley is a wheel with a rope. It lets you pull down to lift something up. Many ropes can make the pull smaller.

example.q: A stone is heavy. How can a long stick help to lift it?
steps: Put a small rock under the stick as a pivot.
Put one end of the stick under the stone.
Push down on the far end of the stick. The stone lifts.
example.a: Use the stick as a lever with a pivot

analogies.home: A claw hammer pulls out a nail like a lever.
analogies.city: A crane uses pulleys to lift building parts.
analogies.farm: A well uses a rope and pulley to bring up water.
analogies.sport: A seesaw in the park is a lever.

terms: A stiff bar that turns on a pivot.
The point a lever turns on.
A wheel with a rope around it.
The push or pull you give.

misc.right: A long lever on your side needs less push.

stages.limits: A pulley with many ropes needs less pull but more rope.

trip.prompt: Find three kinds of lever in the pictures. Which one is a seesaw?

questions.q: What is the pivot of a seesaw?
o: The middle point it turns on
The seat that the child sits on
The child who sits on it
questions.why: The pivot is the point the bar turns around.

questions.q: Which is a lever?
questions.why: A seesaw is a bar turning on a pivot.

questions.q: A pulley is a wheel with what?
questions.why: The rope runs over the wheel.

questions.q: You want to lift a heavy stone with a stick. Where should you push?
questions.why: A long arm on your side means a smaller push.

questions.q: A pulley on a flag pole helps you to do what?
o: Pull down to lift the flag up
Cut the rope in two pieces
questions.why: A pulley changes the direction of the pull.

questions.q: A big child sits near the pivot of a seesaw. A small child sits at the far end. What can happen?
o: The small child cannot go up
questions.why: A short distance with big weight can balance a long distance with small weight.

questions.q: A claw hammer pulls out a nail. Why does a long handle help?
o: A long handle needs less push
A long handle is much lighter
It makes the nail glow in the dark
questions.why: The handle is a long lever arm.

questions.q: A well rope goes over a wheel. What is this?
questions.why: A wheel with a rope is a pulley.

questions.q: Put the lifting steps in order.
items: Put the pivot under the bar
Slide the bar under the stone
Push down on the far end
questions.why: The pivot goes first, then the bar, then the push.

questions.q: Match the tool to what it does.
pairs: Goes up and down on a pivot
questions.why: Levers and pulleys help us lift in different ways.

panel.q: Why does a door handle sit far from the hinge?
o: A longer arm needs less push to turn it
The hinge gets too hot to touch
It saves paint on the door
panel.why: The hinge is the pivot, and the far handle gives a long arm.

panel.q: If you push very near the pivot of a lever, what happens?
panel.why: A short arm gives little help.

panel.q: A pulley makes a pull go down but the load go up. What did it change?
panel.why: A fixed pulley only changes direction of the pull.

teach.topic: How a lever helps us lift
teach.model: A lever is a bar that turns on a pivot. If you push at the long end, you need less push to lift a heavy thing at the short end. A seesaw is a lever.

points.ask: What is a lever made of?
What does it turn on?
Where should I push to make it easy?
Can you give me an example?

stages.title: Wheels and axles
stages.hook: Why is it easier to roll a heavy box on wheels than to drag it? Try to imagine pulling it both ways.
explain: A wheel is a round disc. An axle is the rod through its middle. The wheel turns around the axle.
Rolling rubs less than dragging. Rubbing is called friction. It slows things down and makes them hot.
A big wheel on a small axle gives a big move for a small turn. A steering wheel is a wheel and axle.
Oil or grease on the axle makes the rubbing smaller. Bikes need oil on the chain and hubs.

example.q: Which is easier to move across the floor: a box dragged, or the same box on wheels?
steps: Dragging makes a lot of rubbing.
Wheels roll, so there is less rubbing.
Less rubbing means a smaller push.

analogies.home: A door knob is a small wheel and axle.
analogies.farm: A wheelbarrow has one wheel on an axle.

terms: The rod the wheel turns on.

misc.right: Wheels have friction, but rolling has much less than dragging.

stages.limits: Wheels do not help on soft sand or deep mud. They can sink.

trip.prompt: Find a picture of an old wheel. What is it made of?

questions.q: What is an axle?
o: The rod a wheel turns on
The rubber tyre on the rim
questions.why: The axle goes through the middle of the wheel.

questions.q: Why do wheels help carry heavy things?
o: Rolling has less rubbing than dragging
They make heavy things weigh nothing at all
questions.why: Less friction means less push is needed.

questions.q: What does grease do on an axle?
questions.why: Grease is slippery so surfaces slide easily.

questions.q: A door knob is a wheel and axle. Turning the big knob turns what?
o: The hinge on the door frame
questions.why: The knob is the wheel and the rod is the axle.

questions.q: A cart's wheels squeak and are hard to turn. What is a good fix?
o: Add oil or grease to the axle
Take the axle out completely and push
questions.why: Squeaking shows high friction. Oil reduces it.

questions.q: Why do we not make wheels square?
o: Squares are too expensive to make
Squares are too light to carry
Squares are not allowed by law
questions.why: A round wheel keeps its centre at the same height as it rolls.

questions.q: Which has a wheel and axle?
questions.why: A wheelbarrow wheel turns on an axle.

questions.q: A steering wheel is large. Why?
o: A big wheel is easier to turn
It is prettier to look at
questions.why: A big wheel gives a long arm so the turn needs less push.

questions.q: Put the things in order from most rubbing to least rubbing when moving a box.
questions.why: Smoother surfaces and rolling lower friction.

questions.q: Match each part to its job.
questions.why: Each part helps the wheel to work.

panel.q: Why does a bike chain get oil?
o: To make it heavy and slow
panel.why: Oil lowers friction and keeps parts from wearing out.

panel.q: A cart has a very thin broken axle. What is the danger?
o: It can snap and the wheel falls off
It makes the cart go faster
Nothing, thin axles never break at all
panel.why: The axle holds the load, so a weak one is unsafe.

panel.q: Which wheel needs the smallest turn to move a long way?
panel.why: A bigger wheel goes farther in one turn.

teach.topic: Why wheels help us move things
teach.model: A wheel is round and turns on an axle. Rolling has less rubbing than dragging, so a heavy thing is easier to move. For example, a wheelbarrow carries heavy sand easily.

points.ask: What is a wheel and axle?
Why is rolling easier than dragging?
How can we make it roll even better?
Where do I see this?

stages.title: Gears and motion
stages.hook: Look at a bike. When you pedal slowly, the back wheel can spin fast. How can that be?
explain: A gear is a wheel with teeth. Teeth of two gears fit together.
When one gear turns, it pushes the next one. The next gear turns the other way.
A small gear turns faster than a big gear that it touches. A big gear turns slower but pushes harder.
Gears can change speed, push or direction. Clocks, bikes and drills use gears.

example.q: Two gears touch. Gear A turns clockwise. Which way does gear B turn?
steps: The teeth push each other.
One goes one way.
The other goes the opposite way.

analogies.home: A hand whisk has gears that spin the blades.
analogies.farm: A tractor gearbox helps it pull heavy loads.
analogies.sport: A bike has gears for hills.

stages.mnemonic: Teeth meet, turns repeat, opposite way.
terms: A box of gears in a machine.
A loop that links two gears.

misc.wrong: Touching gears turn the same way.
misc.right: Touching gears turn in opposite directions.

stages.limits: Gears wear out if they are not oiled.

trip.prompt: Find a picture of two gears meshing. Which way does each one turn?

questions.q: What is a gear?
questions.why: The teeth lock together with other gears.

questions.q: Two gears touch. One turns clockwise. The other turns what way?
questions.why: Touching gears turn in opposite directions.

questions.q: Which turns faster when the two touch?
questions.why: A small gear has fewer teeth, so it goes round more times.

questions.q: A bike goes up a steep hill. Which gear helps?
o: A low gear that is easy to pedal
The hardest gear on the whole bike
questions.why: A low gear gives more push at the wheel for less pedal effort.

questions.q: A gear tooth breaks. What happens?
o: The gear may slip and jam
The gear gets bigger and stronger
questions.why: Teeth carry the push, so a broken tooth cannot pass it on.

questions.q: Which uses gears?
questions.why: Clocks use gears to move the hands.

questions.q: Three gears are in a row, touching. Gear 1 turns clockwise. Gear 3 turns which way?
questions.why: Gear 2 turns anticlockwise, then gear 3 turns clockwise again.

questions.q: Why do we put oil in a gearbox?
o: To make it louder than before
questions.why: Oil lets teeth slide and not wear down.

questions.q: Put the gears from fastest turning to slowest turning when linked.
questions.why: Smaller gears turn faster than bigger linked gears.

questions.q: Match each to what it does.
questions.why: Each part has a job in the gear set.

panel.q: A small gear drives a big gear. What does the big gear do?
o: Turns slower but with more push
Turns at the same speed with the same push
panel.why: Speed is traded for turning force.

panel.q: A toy car gearbox gets very hot and smells. What is the best action?
o: Stop and let it cool, then check for rubbing
Keep going and make it run faster
Cover it with a thick blanket
Put it in a bag and keep playing
panel.why: Heat from friction is a warning of a fault.

panel.q: Why might two gears with different tooth sizes not mesh?
o: The teeth would not fit together
They are too cheap to turn
They are too round to touch each other
panel.why: Gears must have matching teeth.

teach.model: A gear is a wheel with teeth. When two gears touch, they turn in opposite ways. A small gear turns faster than a big one. A bike uses gears to help us climb hills.

points.ask: What does a gear look like?
How do two touching gears turn?
Which turns faster?
Where can I find gears?

stages.title: Forces and balance
stages.hook: Why does a tall tower of blocks fall, but a wide one stands? Guess before you read.
explain: A force is a push or a pull. We feel forces when we lift a bag or push a door.
Gravity is a force that pulls everything down to the ground.
Forces can balance. A book on a table is pulled down by gravity and pushed up by the table. Both are equal, so it stays still.
A wide base is steadier than a narrow one. A low heavy part also makes things steadier.

example.q: A book rests on a table. Why does it not fall?
steps: Gravity pulls the book down.
The table pushes the book up.
The two forces are equal, so the book stays still.

analogies.home: A chair with four legs stands better than one with a single leg.
analogies.city: A tall building has a wide strong base.
analogies.farm: A full milk bucket is hard to carry on one side because it tilts you.
analogies.sport: A gymnast on a wide beam stays balanced.

stages.mnemonic: Wide and low, less tip over.
terms: The pull that brings things down.
When forces are equal and nothing moves.
The part at the bottom that a thing stands on.

misc.wrong: A still object has no forces on it.
misc.right: A still object can have equal forces that balance.

stages.limits: Balance depends on where the weight is, as well as how big it is.

trip.prompt: Find a picture of a balanced rock or a seesaw. What forces do you see?

questions.q: What is a force?
questions.why: Forces make things start, stop or change.

questions.q: What does gravity do?
questions.why: Gravity pulls things toward the ground.

questions.q: A book rests on a table. The table pushes it up. Why does it stay still?
o: The up and down forces are equal
There is no gravity on tables
The book is too small to fall
The table is too hot to move it
questions.why: Balanced forces give no change in motion.

questions.q: Which tower is hardest to knock over?
questions.why: A wide base keeps the weight inside the base.

questions.q: You carry a heavy bucket in one hand. What do you do to stay steady?
questions.why: You move your weight to balance the bucket.

questions.q: Why do bridges and tall buildings have wide bases?
o: To stay steady and not tip
To keep warm on cold days
questions.why: A wide base makes them stable.

questions.q: A tug-of-war has two teams pulling equally. What happens?
questions.why: Equal opposite pulls balance.

questions.q: If one team pulls harder, what happens?
o: The rope moves toward the stronger team
The two teams swap places for fun
questions.why: The forces are no longer balanced.

questions.q: Put the shelves from most steady to least steady.
items: Wide, heavy things on the bottom
Wide, light things on the bottom
questions.why: A low heavy part and wide base lower the tip risk.

questions.q: Match each to the force.
questions.why: Forces are pushes, pulls or gravity.

panel.q: A ladder leans on a wall. Why must the feet be on firm flat ground?
o: So it does not slip or tip
So it sings in the wind
panel.why: Firm ground gives grip and balance.

panel.q: A lorry is loaded with heavy boxes on top. What is the danger?
o: It may tip over on a bend
It is too quiet to hear
It is too bright to see at night
None, a high load is safer
panel.why: A high weight makes a vehicle easier to tip.

panel.q: Where should you put heavy things on a shelf?
panel.why: Heavy things low make the shelf steady.

teach.model: A force is a push or a pull. A book on a table is pulled down by gravity and pushed up by the table. Both are equal, so the book stays still. A wide base also helps things stay steady.

points.ask: What is a force?
What pulls the book down?
Why does it stay still?
How can I make a tower steady?

stages.title: Materials and mechanical objects
stages.hook: Why are bike frames made of metal but windows made of glass? What does each material do well?
explain: Materials are what things are made of. Wood, metal, plastic, glass and rubber are materials.
Each has different features. Metal is strong. Rubber stretches. Glass is clear but can break. Wood is light and can be cut.
Engineers choose a material to fit the job. A cooking pot needs a metal that handles heat. A tyre needs rubber to grip.
Some materials bend and come back. This is called springy. Others snap. This is called brittle.

example.q: Which material is best for a spoon to stir hot soup: metal, wood or ice?
steps: Ice would melt.
Metal gets hot and may burn the hand.
Wood stays cooler and is strong enough.

analogies.home: A rubber glove stretches. A glass cup breaks if dropped.
analogies.farm: A fence uses wood or wire.
analogies.sea: A boat hull must be strong and keep out water.

terms: What a thing is made of.

misc.wrong: One material is best for everything.
misc.right: Each material is good for some jobs and bad for others.

stages.limits: A material may be strong in one way and weak in another.

trip.prompt: Find three materials and say what each is good for.

questions.q: What is a material?
o: What a thing is made of
A kind of cloud in the sky
questions.why: Wood, metal and glass are materials.

questions.q: Which material stretches?
questions.why: Rubber is stretchy, so it is used in bands and tyres.

questions.q: Why are tyres made of rubber?
o: It grips the road and absorbs bumps
It is clear so you can see through it
It is brittle and snaps easily
questions.why: Rubber is springy and grippy.

questions.q: Why is a cooking pot made of metal?
o: It is clear like a window
questions.why: Metal conducts heat and does not burn.

questions.q: You need to build a shelter from rain with things nearby. Which is a good roof material?
o: Sand in a bag with holes
questions.why: A roof must keep water out.

questions.q: Glass is hit by a hammer. What usually happens?
questions.why: Glass is brittle.

questions.q: Why would we not make a bridge from paper?
questions.why: A bridge must carry heavy loads.

questions.q: A toy car needs wheels that last. Which is best?
questions.why: Chocolate melts, ice melts and cloth wears.

questions.q: Put these in order from most bendy to most stiff.
questions.why: Rubber stretches most. Steel is stiffest.

questions.q: Match the material to its good use.
questions.why: Each material suits a different job.

panel.q: A child's toy has to be safe if it is chewed. What should engineers avoid?
o: Large pieces that cannot be swallowed
panel.why: Small parts can be swallowed. Paint must be safe.

panel.q: Why use steel for a crane arm?
panel.why: A crane carries heavy loads.

panel.q: A material is strong but heavy. When is it a poor choice?
panel.why: A kite must be light.

teach.model: Materials are what things are made of. Metal is strong, rubber stretches and glass is clear. Engineers choose the right material for the job. For example, a tyre is rubber so it grips the road.

points.ask: Can you name a material?
What is it good at?
How do we pick one?
Can you give me an example?

stages.title: Building simple mechanisms
stages.hook: Can you make a tiny crane from sticks, string and a cup? Think what parts you need.
explain: A mechanism is a set of parts that work together to move something.
Think first: what should it do? Then pick the parts. A crane needs a frame, a rope and a hook.
Build in small steps and test each step. If a part does not move, look for rubbing or a loose joint.
Use safe tools. Ask a grown-up to help with scissors or glue. Keep fingers away from moving parts.

example.q: You want a toy lift to raise a cup with a string. What do you do?
steps: Build a frame with a pulley at the top.
Tie the string to the cup and run it over the pulley.
Pull the string down and the cup goes up.
example.a: Use a pulley on a frame

analogies.home: A drawer slides on rails and has a handle.
analogies.city: A level crossing barrier is a lever.
analogies.farm: A hand pump moves water with a lever.
analogies.music: A piano key is a lever that hits a string.

terms: Parts that work together to move something.
The part that holds things in place.

misc.wrong: A first try should work perfectly.
misc.right: Testing and fixing are a normal part of building.

stages.limits: Cardboard models can show an idea but are not strong enough for real loads.

trip.prompt: Find a mechanism with a lever and a wheel. What does it move?

questions.q: What is a mechanism?
o: Parts that work together to move something
A kind of paint for metal
A shop that sells machines and tools to people
questions.why: Levers, gears and wheels combine in mechanisms.

questions.q: What do you do first when building?
questions.why: The goal tells you which parts you need.

questions.q: A wheel on your toy car will not turn. What may be wrong?
o: Too much rubbing at the axle
The car is going too fast for it
questions.why: Friction or a bent axle stops a wheel.

questions.q: What is a prototype?
questions.why: A prototype lets us test ideas cheaply.

questions.q: Who should help you with sharp scissors?
questions.why: Sharp tools need care and help.

questions.q: Your toy crane tips over when it lifts. What can you do?
o: Make the base wider and heavier
questions.why: A wide heavy base stops tipping.

questions.q: Why do we test each step?
questions.why: Small steps make faults easy to find.

questions.q: A drawer slides easily on rails. What helps it?
questions.why: Smooth surfaces mean low friction.

questions.q: Put the building steps in order.
questions.why: Plan, build, test, then improve.

questions.q: Match each part to what it does in a toy crane.
questions.why: Each part has a job in the crane.

panel.q: Your toy gate does not close. What is a good way to find the fault?
o: Test each joint one by one
Pull hard on everything at once
panel.why: Checking one by one finds the cause.

panel.q: Why use a pulley rather than lifting a cup by hand on a tall frame?
o: You can pull down from a safe, easy place
It is slower than lifting by hand
It makes the cup heavier to lift
panel.why: A pulley changes the direction of the pull.

panel.q: A string snaps when lifting a heavy cup. What next?
panel.why: The load was too big for the string.

teach.topic: How to build a simple mechanism
teach.model: A mechanism is a set of parts that work together. First decide what it should do. Then build a little at a time and test it. For example, a toy crane uses a frame, string and a pulley to lift a cup.

points.ask: What is a mechanism?
What do I do first?
What if it does not work?
What could I build?

stages.title: Introduction to engineering drawings
stages.hook: How can you show a builder exactly what a toy car should look like without words? Try drawing it from the top and the side.
explain: An engineering drawing is a plan that shows how to make something. It uses lines, shapes and numbers.
Draw the same thing from the front, the top and the side. Each view shows a different part.
Numbers show the size. They are often in millimetres (mm) or centimetres (cm).
Lines have jobs. A solid line is an edge you can see. A dashed line shows an edge that is hidden.

example.q: A drawing shows a box 40 mm wide. A dashed line is inside it. What does the dashed line show?
steps: Solid lines are edges you can see.
Dashed lines are edges you cannot see.
So the dashed line is a hidden edge, like a hole inside.

analogies.home: A recipe or a map tells you how to do things.
analogies.city: A city map shows where streets go.
analogies.farm: A plan of a barn shows where doors go.
analogies.tech: A computer program can draw a plan.

stages.mnemonic: Solid you see, dashed is hidden.
terms: A plan that shows how to make something.
One side of the thing, such as front or top.
How much smaller a drawing is than the real thing.

misc.wrong: A drawing is just a pretty picture.
misc.right: A drawing has exact sizes and lines so others can make the part.

stages.limits: Different countries may use different drawing styles, but the idea is the same.

trip.prompt: Find a drawing with front, top and side views. Which view is which?

questions.q: Why do engineers make drawings?
o: To show others how to make something
questions.why: A drawing tells makers shapes and sizes.

questions.q: A dashed line usually shows what?
questions.why: Hidden parts are drawn with dashes.

questions.q: What do numbers on a drawing show?
questions.why: Dimensions tell the builder the size.

questions.q: Why show a top view and a side view?
o: Each shows parts the other cannot
To hide the shape of the part
questions.why: One view may hide details.

questions.q: A drawing says 50 mm. What do you measure with?
questions.why: mm measures length.

questions.q: A map of a room is drawn smaller than the room. What is this called?
questions.why: Scale shows how much smaller the drawing is.

questions.q: A hole goes through a block. How might the top view show the hole?
questions.why: Looking down a round hole shows a circle.

questions.q: Why must the sizes on a drawing be exact?
questions.why: Mistakes make parts that do not fit.

questions.q: Put these steps for making a drawing in order.
questions.why: Observe, sketch, measure, check.

questions.q: Match the line to its meaning.
questions.why: Drawing marks follow set rules.

panel.q: Two workers make the same part from one drawing in different towns. Why do they get the same result?
o: The drawing uses agreed rules and exact sizes
They talk all day on the phone
They use magic to copy it
panel.why: Shared rules let everyone read the same plan.

panel.q: A drawing is 1 cm for each 10 cm in real life. A line is 3 cm on paper. How long is the real part?
A drawing has no sizes. What is the problem?
o: The maker cannot know how big to make it
It is too clear to read
It is too big for the page
panel.why: Sizes are needed for making.

teach.model: An engineering drawing is a plan that shows how to make something. It has lines for edges and numbers for sizes. It shows the top, front and side. For example, a drawing of a toy car tells a maker how long to cut each part.

points.ask: What is a drawing for?
What does it show?
How do you know how big?
Can you give me an example?
